newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian plane to Turkey crashes, 50 dead.
newsitem.headline: Russian plane to Turkey crashes, 50 dead.

text.p: Fifty passengers and crew aboard a southern Russian regional aircraft died when the AN-24 plane crashed on Tuesday en route to Turkey, officials said.
It was the worst domestic disaster for Russia's troubled airline industry in more than a year.
The charter Stavropol Airlines flight crashed 37 minutes after take off from Stavropol to Trabzon on Turkey's northern coast, Pyotr Markin, an assistant to the airline's director, said by telephone.

"We believe the plan caught fire in mid air and fell down into a forest...Nobody heard the blast," said Vladimir Konnonov, the duty officer of the local emergency committee. "Rescue teams say nobody survived."
Markin said there were 41 passengers and nine crew on board.
"Air traffic control did not receive any information from the crew about any dangers, but then the plane disappeared from the radar screen, ending communications," Markin said.
By late afternoon rescuers had recovered 24 bodies, which were scattered across a large field, Sergei Berezin, deputy mayor of Cherkessk near the crash site, said by telephone.
Markin said the plane's flight recorder had been found in good condition.

Interfax news agency quoted regional governor Vladimir Khubiyev as saying the accident could have been caused by an explosion on board the plane. Human remains and wreckage were spread across a three km (two mile) area.

Zulfa Batasheva, a regional public prosecutor, told Reuters that the tail was found 1.5 km (one mile) away from the rest of the wreck, raising the possibility that the plane fell apart in midair. She added a criminal investigation had been opened as in other air crashes.
However local police official Murat Baibagisov, contacted by telephone, said an eyewitness to the crash saw no explosion, just smoke.

Markin said it was too early to comment on the cause of the crash in a forest near the North Caucasus town of Cherkessk, capital of the ethnic region of Karachayevo-Cherkessiya neighbouring Stavropol region.
But he ruled out the weather -- it was snowing at the time of the crash -- as a factor.
Officials said most if not all passengers were Russian "shuttle traders" who buy goods abroad to resell at home.
Russia's air safety standards have fallen since Soviet monopoly Aeroflot was split into hundreds of smaller domestic companies after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Many of them are struggling financially, forcing them to take shortcuts in maintenence and safety standards, experts say.
The government-owned Rossiiskaya Gazeta daily newspaper said earlier this week that 219 people died last year in 43 air accidents in Russian air space, 14 of them major.
Most air accidents occur on take off or landing. During Tuesday's flight however, the plane was nearly midway on its route at its cruising altitude of 6,000 meters (19,000 feet), Markin said.
The ageing AN-24 is an outdated 52-seat propeller plane used for short and medium distance flights.
The crash was the worst in Russia since December 1995, when 97 died in a air disaster in the Russian Far East. A crash of a Vnukovo Airlines flight in Norway killed 140 last August.
